newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon seen pressured by Boeing deal.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon seen pressured by Boeing deal.

text.p: Raytheon Co found itself under increasing pressure to ink a merger deal with GM Hughes Electronics Corp or another big defense contractor in the wake of Boeing Co's proposed acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp, analysts said on Monday.

"It certainly pushes Raytheon closer to doing something," J.P. Morgan analyst Roger Threlfaal said in a telephone interview, adding that talks between Lexington-based Raytheon and had resumed several weeks ago.
He has a buy recommendation out on both companies.

Executives at Raytheon, the largest private employer in Massachusetts with $12 billion in sales for 1995, have long talked about reaching "a critical mass." They had been in discussions with both McDonnell Douglas and Los Angeles-based GM Hughes earlier this year. But talks with each firm broke down.

"With the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas deal, Raytheon now has a short-term window (for completing a deal with GM Hughes). It's not a long-term window. It will probably last until the (Boeing-McDonnell) deal is closed," Cowen & Co's analyst Cai Von Rumohr said.

"It's a dynamic situation," said Von Rumohr, who has rated Raytheon neutral. "The folks at Hughes aren't stupid. They're not offering a price cut. And if they wait until the deal is done, there will certainly be an entity out there with more than enough cash capable of making the buy."

Threlfall said that while he thought Raytheon and GM-Hughes deal would be the best fit, "it's not the only fit" and suggested that Los Angeles-headquartered Northrop Grumman could also work well. He has a buy rating on Northrop.
"There are problems with both and upsides to both. There can be tax liabilities depending on how GM unwinds Hughes and Northrop has a fair amount of debt on its books," Threlfall said.

Raytheon vice president Bob McQuade declined to comment about possible mergers and acquisitions or talks, but said, "We are committed to maintaining our strategy of being a multi-industry, diversified company. And we are committed to remaining a top-tier player in the defense industry."

In recent years, Raytheon has sought to diversify its businesses by expanding into commerical, engineering and construction and major appliances as a way of blunting the cuts in U.S. defense spending. McQuade noted that more than 60 percent of the company's revenues comes "from multi-industry, commercial business" other than defense.
